item.title: Japan’s Real Baby Bump Is All Relative
item.description: Did Japan just experience its first baby bump in a decade?
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: Did Japan just experience its first baby bump in a decade?For years, it has been the poster child for low fertility, with births falling every year since 2015. But in the first six months of 2026, there was an unexpected uptick: Births of Japanese nationals rose 0.4%, or 1,379 more than in the same period in 2025. Some supporters of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi were quick to claim this as more evidence that she’s restoring the country to its former glory; others noted that, since she took office only in October 2025, all these babies were conceived under her predecessor.Coming in the year of the hinoe uma, the Fire Horse of the Chinese zodiac, it seems impressive. The last such year, 1966, put a massive dent in births thanks to a bygone superstition that girls born in the year of the Fire Horse made poor wives .But it’s certainly no sea change. In fact, the blip might be over. Births in Japan are closely linked to marriages and those are down again this year after rising for the past two years in a rebound from Covid, which suppressed encounters of all kinds. The increase is also tiny next to the more than 14% jump in births next door in South Korea.However, there is a win hiding in plain sight in Japan’s data. As the earliest industrialized country to suffer falling births, Japan remains synonymous with the problem worldwide. But in recent years almost all of the developed world has followed, including several of its neighbors, where the decline has been faster and steeper. As a result, Japan is now the surprising outlier among East Asia’s richest economies. It has the highest fertility rate of the group, at 1.14. All of its peers have fallen below 1. A rate of around 2.1 is needed to hold population levels steady.For years, many assumed that Japan’s low figure was the floor. Now the obvious question is what kept the fertility rate from tumbling below one — and are there lessons for the world in what looks like, if not success, then at least a lesser degree of failure?As the trend of falling births spreads beyond Asia, it’s important to find an answer. One analysis comparing only Japan and South Korea noted that Japanese women marry younger , perhaps due in part to Korea’s expensive weddings, which traditionally include a large lump-sum housing deposit. In both countries, children are overwhelmingly born in wedlock.Another paper, published this year, found that the two countries mirrored each other for years but began to diverge in the early 2000s. That gap stems largely from a drop in births to Korean women in their late 20s, something that did not happen in Japan, and which the authors link to a larger number of young Korean men not employed. In other words, the longer young people have to scrape by, the more fertile years are lost. That is intuitively sound, though it doesn’t tell the whole story: Singapore marries at around the same age as Japan, yet the city-state’s fertility rate is just 0.87.Takaichi supporters are jumping the gun by claiming this as a win. The prime minister herself has declared no such victory; she has described population decline as a “quietly advancing national crisis,” and is compiling a comprehensive strategy to tackle it. It’s also a very regional victory: The gain is entirely due to Tokyo, which Governor Yuriko Koike attributes to her generous support policies, but which may simply reflect that young families who once would have moved to leafier environs outside of the capital are staying put instead.Japan should take the win nonetheless. It's policies are unlikely to stem the downward trend in births, but look at what they have done: The share of working women who stay in their jobs after a first child has risen from about 50% to almost 70%. Daycare waiting lists are largely a thing of the past. Men taking parental leave has soared from under 3% in 2015 to over 50% today. Japan has set itself a frankly unachievable fertility goal of 1.8; measured against that, any policy will fail. Compare that with other countries in the same situation, however, and things start to look a little better. Even Tokyo’s rate, which is the lowest in Japan, is 50% higher than Seoul’s.Sixty years ago, the Fire Horse scared off a quarter of Japan’s births, yet this year it barely registered. One superstition about babies has finally died. The next should be the idea that the country is the world’s demographic basket case.More From Bloomberg Opinion: This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan. item.title: US Intel Helped Nab Mexico Cartel Leader Without Agents on Site
item.description: The US provided intelligence leading to the capture of a suspected Mexican drug kingpin, but no US agents took part in the deadly operation, according to Mexico’s government.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- The US provided intelligence leading to the capture of a suspected Mexican drug kingpin, but no US agents took part in the deadly operation, according to Mexico’s government. Elite Mexican security forces arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores on Saturday following an exchange of heavy gunfire around his compound in Sinaloa state. Known as “El Chapo Isidro,” Meza-Flores is accused of smuggling massive amounts of fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine into the US over more than two decades.He faces extradition to the US after being listed as one of the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives.At her regular morning press conference on Monday, President Claudia Sheinbaum emphasized that the operation was planned and led by Mexican forces, without the participation of US agents on the ground.“The areas in which we coordinate with the US are security and intelligence. That was the agreement we reached from the start,” she said. “But they do not conduct operations in Mexico.” Sheinbaum, however, did confirm that Mexican officials requested that the US deploy a drone to help with the operation, without providing further details.Washington has not claimed responsibility for the strike. Instead, officials celebrated joint coordination on the arrest, including US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson, who pointed to intelligence sharing in a post on X.The arrest of Meza-Flores marks Mexico’s highest-profile cartel operation since the February capture of Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, the longtime leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. Oseguera died from his injuries while he was being transported to a hospital following a military raid.In the operation over the weekend, Mexican security forces killed 16 alleged associates of Meza-Flores, and detained another 16, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla said at the same press conference. More bodies were found after officials originally reported that seven suspected gang members were killed along with four soldiers.Another ten federal agents were injured in the operation that mobilized hundreds of troops, special forces and several Black Hawk helicopters, Trevilla added.Meza-Flores headed the Guasave Cartel, which takes its name from a city in Sinaloa state. The group has trafficked drugs into the US since at least 2000 while more recently fighting a turf war against a faction of the larger Sinaloa Cartel, according to the US Treasury Department.The US government had offered a $5 million reward for information leading to Meza-Flores’ arrest or conviction. Under his leadership, his gang was allied with the Sinaloa Cartel faction led by the family of Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, the veteran Mexican drug lord who co-founded the larger criminal organization decades ago with Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán. Both are serving life sentences in US prisons.Over the past two years, Sheinbaum has faced intense pressure from US President Donald Trump to take more aggressive action against the country’s powerful drug cartels.After a meeting with Sheinbaum in China last week, Trump reiterated that the cartels are “running Mexico,” an assertion the Mexican leader rejects.--With assistance from Michael O'Boyle.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.
